text: At fourteen minutes past six on a Monday evening, Remmy Hale would have given anything to have that morning back.
asr: At 14 minutes past six on a Monday evening, Remy Hale would have given anything to have that morning back.

text: Pip! Pip!
asr: Pit. Pit.

text: She was about to get it.
Twelve hours earlier. Remmy had one job that Monday: to be on time.
asr: 12 hours earlier, Remy had one job that Monday to be on time.

text: Seven o'clock, Monday morning. Rain by six.
Seven forty? No. No, no, no!
asr: 740? No. No. No. No. No.

text: Remi! Will you watch me ride at the park? Six o'clock!
asr: Ready? Will you watch me ride at the park? 6 o'clock

text: Can't, Pip. Big day. Sorry.
She missed the tram. Then she missed the next one.
You're forty minutes late, Ms Hale.
asr: Your 40 minutes late, Ms. Hale.

text: Tell me. If you could build anything at all, what would you build?
I... um. I'm sorry. I don't know.
asr: E-Om. I'm sorry. I don't know.

text: We'll be in touch.
They would not be in touch.
On the way home it rained, and Remmy ducked into a clock shop she had never noticed before.
asr: On the way home it rained and Remy ducked into a clock shop she had never noticed before.

text: Ah. A bad day. I have just the thing.
Turn this knob before you sleep, and you'll wake up to the same morning. Seven turns. After that, it's only a clock.
How much?
Whatever you think a day is worth.
One of the first alarm clocks in America was built in seventeen eighty-seven. It could only ring at four in the morning, the hour its maker got up for work.
asr: One of the first alarm clocks in America was built in 1787. It could only ring at four in the morning, the hour its maker got up for work.

text: Remmy's could do something stranger. She turned the knob.
asr: Remy's could do something stranger. She turned the knob.

text: Seven o'clock, Monday morning. Rain by six.
Monday. Again.
About two in three people say they have felt deja vu at least once. Remmy was feeling it on purpose.
asr: About two in three people say they have felt déjà vu at least once. Remy was feeling it on purpose.

text: Your body keeps its own clock: about twenty thousand nerve cells, just above the place where your optic nerves cross.
asr: Your body keeps its own clock, about 20,000 nerve cells, just above the place where your optic nerves cross.

text: Left alone, it runs about eleven minutes longer than a day. Every morning, the light puts it right again.
Remi! Will you watch me ride at the park? Six o'clock!
asr: Ready? Will you watch me ride at the park? 6 o'clock

text: Big day, Pip. Next time.
So she practised Monday.
asr: So, she practiced Monday.

text: A bridge. No. A tower?
Once you know how something turns out, it feels as if you knew it all along. Psychologists call it hindsight bias.
Remmy didn't just feel it. She really did know.
asr: Remy didn't just feel it, she really did know.

text: A school where every classroom gets the morning sun.
Ms Hale, that's the best answer I've heard all year. Come back at five. The director wants to meet you.
asr: Ms Hale, that's the best answer I've heard all year. Come back at 5. The director wants to meet you.

text: Yes! I mean, yes. Thank you.
The final round ran late. Remmy didn't look at the time. It was the perfect Monday.
asr: The final round ran late, Remy didn't look at the time, it was the perfect Monday.

text: At home, Pip had made her a good luck card. And Pip knew the way to the tram stop.
This is my fault. This is all my fault.
Pip would be all right, the doctors said. In time. But Remmy still had turns left.
asr: Pip would be alright, the doctors said, in time, but Remy still had turns left.

text: That night, she turned the knob with shaking hands.
Pip. Promise me you'll stay home tonight. Promise.
Okay, okay! I promise.
Pick up. Pip, pick up.
Pip kept her promise. Until she saw the rain, and remembered her sister had no umbrella.
It keeps happening! Whatever I change, it happens at fourteen past six!
Because you keep the day you wanted, and only try to change the ending.
A day isn't a recording, miss. It's a promise. You only get to choose who it's for.
Every night, your brain replays the day by itself. In rats, scientists watched brain cells repeat the routes of the day while the animals slept.
Replaying is the easy part. Choosing is hard.
This is the last Monday I can fix.
Then don't fix it. Live it.
Remi! Will you watch me ride at the park? Six o'clock!
asr: Ready? Will you watch me ride at the park? 6 o'clock

text: Six o'clock. I'll be there. I promise.
Really?
Come back at five. The director wants to meet you.
I'm sorry. I can't. I made a promise.
Then I'm afraid there won't be a second chance.
I know.
Pip, wait!
Whoa. That was close.
You came!
I'll always come.
That night, Remmy had one turn left. She didn't take it.
asr: That night Remy had one turn left, she didn't take it.

text: Seven o'clock, Tuesday morning. Sunny all day.
Tuesday.
Ms Hale, it's Halden Architects. The director heard why you left. She'd like to meet you on Thursday.
asr: Miss Hale, it's Hal Den Architects. The director heard why you left. She'd like to meet you on Thursday.

text: Remmy never turned the knob again. She didn't need to.
asr: Remy never turned the knob again, she didn't need to.

text: You can't rewind a day. But every morning, you get to choose who it's for.
